definition.text: This card's own subtitle bundles four concerns -- schedule, durable state, route, handoff -- that this repo's own target facts already keep as separate capability rows. Dispatch is defined narrowly: "one unit of agent work executes and returns one result" (F-b5-02). Durable execution and scheduling are each named as their own capability row with their own adapter and swap-candidate columns (F-b3-04, F-b3-15), and workflow composition is a fifth, separate mechanism -- a caller-authored document of operators -- that this repo's own compose-workflow skill treats as its own concern, not part of the dispatch contract.

tools.name: DBOS
tools.note: Named swap candidate (F-b3-04); genuinely different architecture from Temporal, not a clone of it -- it reuses an existing Postgres database as the durability layer instead of running a dedicated server.

evidence.text: DBOS's own site states that installing its library and connecting it to a Postgres database requires "No new infrastructure" -- a materially different architecture from Temporal, which this repo's own inventory records as a dedicated server that must listen on ports `7233`/`8233`, and is currently down.

tools.name: Inngest
tools.note: Named swap candidate (F-b3-04); event-driven model that hides queue/worker machinery from the caller entirely, distinct from Temporal's explicit worker/task-queue model.

evidence.text: Inngest's own current homepage states its event-driven model plainly: "No workers. No queues. No refactoring."

evidence.quote: No workers. No queues. No refactoring.

tools.name: Orkes Conductor
tools.note: A real production composition-operator implementation, not named in this repo's own tables; its operator vocabulary (Switch, Fork, Do While, Wait, ...) is wider than a fixed set of six, which bears on whether a closed six-operator set is representative of the field or this repo's own choice.

evidence.text: Operators are built-in primitives in Conductor that allow you to define the workflow's control flow, similar to programming constructs such as for loops and if-else selections.

evidence.quote: Operators express control flow in the definition itself: fork and join for parallelism, switch for branching, do-while for loops, and sub-workflows for composition.

tools.name: Microsoft Agent Framework (Magentic orchestration)
tools.note: A production multi-agent orchestrator whose control flow is decided dynamically at runtime by a manager, not selected in advance from a fixed, author-declared set of operators -- direct counter-evidence to a closed operator set as the industry norm.

evidence.text: a dedicated Magentic manager coordinates a team of specialized agents, selecting which agent should act next based on the evolving context, task progress, and agent capabilities.

evidence.quote: a dedicated Magentic manager coordinates a team of specialized agents, selecting which agent should act next based on the evolving context, task progress, and agent capabilities.

landscape.text: What a durable-execution/workflow engine actually provides is a journal of every step so a crash can resume without redoing work; this is a class of engine (Temporal, Restate, DBOS, Inngest, plus AWS Step Functions, LangGraph and Cloudflare Workflows named in the same source), and Temporal is one option in it with a materially different architecture from at least one alternative, not the representative design: DBOS's own site describes its setup as "Just install the open-source DBOS library to your code and connect it to a Postgres database. No new infrastructure required." -- unlike Temporal, which this repo's own inventory records as a dedicated server that must listen on ports `7233`/`8233` and is currently down. Separately, whether a closed set of composition operators is how the field actually works is not settled by the evidence gathered here: Orkes Conductor exposes a wider, open-ended operator vocabulary than six, and Microsoft's Magentic orchestration and handoff-pattern orchestration both select the next step dynamically at runtime rather than from an author-fixed graph -- production multi-agent orchestration includes control flow this repo's own closed-set design (marked proposed in compose-workflow's own skill.json) does not represent.

evidence.quote: A durable execution engine ensures reliable, stateful execution of workflows and processes in distributed systems.
Just install the open-source DBOS library to your code and connect it to a Postgres database. No new infrastructure required.

usage.text: This card conflates two different calls this repo otherwise keeps apart. Dispatch's call is deliberately thin: a caller submits one unit of work and gets back one result, and the seam's contract, not an engine's native API, "must specify: the request shape, the result shape, cancellation semantics, timeout and budget enforcement, partial-result handling, and what a failure returns." Composing steps ahead of that call is this repo's own proposed design, not sourced to a PASS/TARGET fact: a caller writes a document whose step is one of six operator objects -- sequence, parallel, bounded loop, approval gate, agent call, judge -- each nesting because a step is itself a document, per compose-workflow's own schema.

evidence.quote: must specify: the request shape, the result shape, cancellation semantics, timeout and budget enforcement, partial-result handling, and what a failure returns

gaps.what: This card's subtitle names four concerns -- schedule, durable state, route (dispatch), handoff (workflow composition) -- that this repo's own architecture already keeps as four separate skills: compose-workflow, cap-scheduling, cap-durable-execution, seam-dispatch. Nothing in the evidence gathered here justifies re-merging them onto one reference-model card.
gaps.why_it_matters: A card that bundles four separately-contracted capabilities invites a caller to think one adapter (Temporal) satisfies all four, when this repo's own design keeps them independently swappable.
gaps.research_query: kb_index.py search "compose-workflow cap-scheduling cap-durable-execution seam-dispatch boundary"

gaps.what: This card names a specific vendor (Temporal) in its subtitle, while this repo's own stated rule elsewhere (cap-model-access) is that a caller requests a class, never a vendor. The reference model gives this card no standard badge, so there is no capability-class vocabulary standing in for the vendor name here the way there is for, e.g., isolation (OCI Runtime Spec).
gaps.why_it_matters: Naming a product in an architecture document that otherwise insists on vendor-neutral class names is inconsistent with this repo's own design rule, and it papers over that durable execution and dispatch each have a real standard-free capability-class definition (F-b3-04, F-b5-02) that does not require naming Temporal at all.
gaps.research_query: does any other 'built' card in the reference model name a specific vendor in its subtitle rather than a capability class

gaps.what: This repo's own current-state inventory (PASS.md A6, "Defined but not running") records Temporal's data directory as present but its server not listening, with durable workflow orchestration and human-in-the-loop signals "designed around it" while it is down. This card is nonetheless marked status: built.
gaps.why_it_matters: A 'built' status resting on a named adapter that is itself recorded elsewhere in this repo as not running is an unevidenced claim for at least the durable-execution and scheduling portions of this card, mirroring the pattern flagged on other 'built' cards where the live path is claimed, not measured.
gaps.research_query: is Temporal listening on 7233/8233 in the current environment, and has any dispatch or durable-execution harness's live adapter run against it

gaps.what: Scheduling may not belong on this card at all. cap-scheduling's own load trigger explicitly warns against "an orchestrator would own recurrence," RFC 5545 recurrence rules is scheduling's own named standard (F-b3-15) and does not appear on this card, and card 1.2 (a Scheduled entry door, per this card's own area map) already exists as a separate address for firing recurring work.
gaps.why_it_matters: If recurrence is computed once, as a pure function of a rule, time zone and window, and enters through the ordinary envelope like any other trigger, folding "schedule" into a workflow-engine card re-introduces the coupling cap-scheduling was written to remove.
gaps.research_query: kb_index.py search "cap-scheduling orchestrator owns recurrence RFC 5545"

gaps.what: Whether dispatch is genuinely separable from the workflow engine in practice is not settled by the evidence gathered here. Even inside Temporal's own architecture, an activity (one unit of work) and the workflow that calls it run on different workers, connected only through the engine's own trace-propagation and task-queue machinery -- Temporal already contains an internal dispatch layer rather than treating it as an externally pluggable seam.
gaps.why_it_matters: If the named adapter for this card does not itself treat dispatch as swappable independent of the workflow engine, this repo's seam-dispatch boundary may be a bucketing choice that a real adapter swap would not respect, and no evidence was found either way from a working integration.
gaps.research_query: has any harness call.py exercised seam-dispatch against Temporal's own activity/task-queue model rather than a dry-run stand-in

gaps.what: No open standard defines the request/result envelope a dispatch call should use. The one governance-backed agent-to-agent standard found (A2A)'s Task object has exactly six fields (id, contextId, status, artifacts, history, metadata) and by explicit design excludes a plan or decomposition field -- "agents collaborate based on declared capabilities and exchanged information, without needing to share their internal thoughts, plans, or tool implementations" -- consistent with this card's own dispatch definition of one opaque, typed result, but that is a convergence this repo has not itself checked its seam-dispatch contract against.
gaps.why_it_matters: If seam-dispatch's request/result shape has never been compared field-by-field against A2A's Task object, a claim that they agree (or a claim that A2A is irrelevant) is unevidenced either way.
gaps.research_query: does seam-dispatch's request/result schema map onto A2A's Task object fields, or diverge, and where

gaps.what: A verification pass found this card previously cited a record (X-cap-durable-execution-006) at two json_paths (the DBOS tool entry and landscape) for a claim that 'DBOS reuses Postgres as the durability layer for workflows, while Temporal runs a dedicated cluster. Restate focuses on providing a lightweight, cloud-native engine...' -- attributed to a Spheron blog post that compares exactly three engines (Temporal, Inngest, Restate) and never mentions DBOS anywhere in the ~5,000-word article (0 occurrences, grepped). The Restate sentence in that same fabricated snippet has been dropped from this card entirely (Restate already has its own separately, cleanly sourced tool entry). The original record is left unedited as the discovered defect; this card now cites a freshly captured DBOS primary source (X-refmodel-2-4-dispatch-001) instead. A second, lower-severity citation (X-entry-composition-028, Inngest) quoted a sentence not found on a fresh capture of the same URL, though the page's current headline and framing do support the underlying claim -- re-sourced to X-refmodel-2-4-dispatch-002.
gaps.why_it_matters: An entire named product (DBOS) with a specific architectural claim attached to it was fabricated relative to its cited page -- the cleanest kind of citation defect, since the page is silent rather than merely paraphrased. A reader who trusted the old citation would have no way to know the comparison never happened on that page.
gaps.research_query: does a future tools/verify_snippets.py pass flag X-cap-durable-execution-006, and should its status be annotated so other cards do not cite it
